Grokster were heard before the Supreme Court March 29, ", "rephrased": "The Supreme Court of the United States recently heard oral arguments in the landmark MGM v. Grokster case, where 28 entertainment companies sued the makers of peer-to-peer software for facilitating copyright infringement. This legal battle centers on whether software developers can be held liable for illegal file-sharing activities, a question that could fundamentally alter the future of digital content distribution in the country.", "summary": "The Supreme Court is deciding if software makers are liable for user copyright infringement via peer-to-peer networks."}, "1": {"original": "The case concerns an appeal of prior rulings favoring Grokster's right to market", "rephrased": "The current legal dispute involves an appeal of previous lower court decisions that ruled in favor of peer-to-peer software companies, despite evidence that the majority of content shared through these networks is distributed without the permission of copyright holders.", "summary": "Lower courts previously ruled that peer-to-peer software companies could legally market their technology even if users used it to infringe copyrights."}, "2": {"original": "The outcome could determine the ultimate fate of P2P software in the U.S.,", "rephrased": "The final ruling in this case will determine whether peer-to-peer software remains legal in the United States, potentially holding technology innovators legally responsible for the unauthorized distribution of copyrighted material by their users.", "summary": "The upcoming Supreme Court decision will decide the legal status of peer-to-peer software and the liability of its creators."}, "3": {"original": "The author cites survey data indicating that 49% of Americans believe file", "rephrased": "Recent survey data reveals that nearly half of the American public believes that companies operating file-sharing networks should be held legally responsible for the music and movie piracy committed by their users, reflecting a strong desire for corporate accountability in the digital age.", "summary": "A significant majority of Americans support holding file-sharing network operators legally responsible for user piracy."}}
